items.title: Absolute convergence, a second proof
items.prose: l13 proved that absolute convergence implies convergence with the Cauchy criterion. Here is a proof by comparison instead. Assume $\sum |a_n|$ converges. Two lines are flawed.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Let $b_n = a_n + |a_n|$. Since $-|a_n| \le a_n \le |a_n|$, we have $0 \le b_n \le 2|a_n|$.
$\sum 2|a_n|$ converges, so by the comparison test $\sum b_n$ converges.
Now $a_n = b_n - |a_n|$, the difference of the terms of two convergent series.
By the difference law for the partial sums, $\sum a_n$ converges. $\blacksquare$
Since $a_n \le |a_n|$, the comparison test gives $\sum a_n$ convergent directly.
lines.why: You compared signed terms. Comparison needs $0 \le a_n$; that is why we shift by $|a_n|$ first.
You chose the wrong sign. $a_n - |a_n| \le 0$; the shifted terms must be $a_n + |a_n|$.

feedback.correct: Right. Shift the terms to make them non-negative, compare, then subtract.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build a non-negative series from $a_n$ and $|a_n|$, compare it, then undo the shift.

byKey.d1: You applied comparison to terms that may be negative.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: $0 \le a_n + |a_n| \le 2|a_n|$, so comparison gives a convergent $\sum (a_n + |a_n|)$. Subtracting the convergent $\sum |a_n|$ term by term leaves $\sum a_n$. This proof uses monotone convergence where l13 used Cauchy; both rest on completeness.

items.title: A ratio test, then the sum
items.prose: For $\sum_{n \ge 1} \tfrac{3^n}{n!}$ the ratios are $\tfrac{3}{n+1} \to 0$, so the series converges. From `taylor`, $e^x = \sum_{n \ge 0} \tfrac{x^n}{n!}$ for every $x$.
items.question: What is $\sum_{n \ge 1} \tfrac{3^n}{n!}$? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The exponential series starts at $n = 0$; this one starts at $n = 1$.

byKey.with0: You included the $n = 0$ term, which is 1. This sum starts at $n = 1$.
byKey.e3over: You divided by 3. The terms are $\tfrac{3^n}{n!}$, exactly those of $e^3$.

explain.text: The ratio test gives convergence, since $L = 0 < 1$. The series is $e^3$ without its first term, 1, so the sum is $e^3 - 1 \approx 19.0855$. Adding 59 terms in Python gives the same value to twelve places.

items.title: A partial sum in closed form
items.question: Give $S_n$ as a formula in $n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Three positive pieces never cancel, and three negative pieces at the end do not either.

byKey.one-tail: You kept one negative survivor. The last three pieces, $-\tfrac1{n+1}$, $-\tfrac1{n+2}$ and $-\tfrac1{n+3}$, all survive.
byKey.one-head: You kept one positive survivor. $1$, $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac13$ all survive, because the negatives start at $-\tfrac14$.

explain.text: The positives are $1, \tfrac12, \dots, \tfrac1n$ and the negatives $\tfrac14, \dots, \tfrac1{n+3}$; all but six cancel. So $S_n = 1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac{1}{n+1} - \tfrac{1}{n+2} - \tfrac{1}{n+3}$. Check $n = 2$: $\tfrac34 + \tfrac{3}{10} = \tfrac{21}{20} = \tfrac{11}{6} - \tfrac13 - \tfrac14 - \tfrac15$.

items.title: How far to sum
items.question: What is the smallest $m$ for which this bound guarantees a tail below 0.0003?

byKey.floor: At $m = 3333$ the bound is $\tfrac{1}{3333} \approx 0.00030003$, just above 0.0003.
byKey.sq: You solved $\tfrac{1}{m^2} < 0.0003$, a bound on one term. The tail of many terms is bounded by $\tfrac1m$.

explain.text: $\tfrac1m < 0.0003$ means $m > \tfrac{10000}{3} \approx 3333.3$, so $m = 3334$. The lower bound $\tfrac{1}{m+1}$ shows the tail is really about 0.0003 there. Tails of $\sum \tfrac1{n^2}$ shrink like $\tfrac1m$, slowly.

items.title: Ratios below 1 are not enough
items.prose: A student 'proves' that $\sum \tfrac1n$ converges. One line is false.

rows: So $a_n \le a_1 r^{n-1}$, and comparison with a geometric series gives convergence.

items.question: Tap the false line.

feedback.correct: Right. The supremum of the ratios is 1.

byKey.r1: Line 2 is true: each ratio is below 1 and the terms are positive.
byKey.r3: Line 4 would follow if line 3 were true. The false claim is earlier.

explain.text: The ratios $\tfrac{n}{n+1}$ creep up to 1, so their supremum is 1, not less. The ratio test needs one fixed $r < 1$ that bounds the ratios past some $N$, which $L < 1$ supplies. Here $L = 1$, and the series diverges.

items.title: What a convergent positive series forces
items.question: Which of these series must converge? Select all that apply.

options.why: You expected roots to stay small. With $a_n = \tfrac1{n^2}$, $\sum \sqrt{a_n} = \sum \tfrac1n$ diverges.
You expected the weights to be harmless. With $a_n = \tfrac1{n^2}$, $\sum n a_n = \sum \tfrac1n$ diverges.

feedback.correct: Right. Four must converge; the root and the weighted series need not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try $a_n = \tfrac{1}{n^2}$ on each, and look for a comparison for the rest.

explain.text: $a_n \to 0$, so eventually $a_n \le 1$ and $a_n^2 \le a_n$; also $\tfrac{a_n}{1 + a_n} \le a_n$ and $a_{2n}$ is part of a non-negative convergent series. $\sum (-1)^n a_n$ converges absolutely. With $a_n = \tfrac{1}{n^2}$, both $\sum \sqrt{a_n}$ and $\sum n a_n$ become $\sum \tfrac1n$.

items.title: Both halves of a conditional series diverge
items.prose: Prove: if $\sum a_n$ converges but $\sum |a_n|$ diverges, then $\sum a_n^+$ and $\sum a_n^-$ both diverge, where $a_n^+ = \max(a_n, 0)$ and $a_n^- = \max(-a_n, 0)$. This is what l14's greedy rule needed. Two lines are flawed.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: For every $n$, $a_n = a_n^+ - a_n^-$ and $|a_n| = a_n^+ + a_n^-$.
Suppose $\sum a_n^+$ converged. Then $\sum a_n^- = \sum (a_n^+ - a_n)$ would converge, by the difference law.
Then $\sum |a_n| = \sum (a_n^+ + a_n^-)$ would converge, by the sum law: a contradiction. So $\sum a_n^+$ diverges.
Swapping the roles of $a_n^+$ and $a_n^-$, the same argument shows $\sum a_n^-$ diverges. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: You read divergence as the terms not tending to 0. $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges with $\tfrac1n \to 0$; and here $a_n \to 0$, since $\sum a_n$ converges.

lines.text: $a_n^+ \le |a_n|$ and $\sum |a_n|$ diverges, so $\sum a_n^+$ diverges by comparison.
lines.why: You passed divergence downwards. Comparison only passes it from a smaller series to a larger one.

feedback.correct: Right. One convergent half would drag the other, and then the sizes, into convergence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Assume one half converges and derive that $\sum |a_n|$ converges.

byKey.d1: The terms do tend to 0 here, because $\sum a_n$ converges.
byKey.d2: Being below a divergent series proves nothing.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: If one half converged, the identity $a_n^- = a_n^+ - a_n$ would make the other converge. Adding them would make $\sum |a_n|$ converge, which it does not. So both halves diverge, which is exactly what lets the greedy rule cross every target.

items.title: Steering below zero
items.prose: Write `rearrange_to(target, n)` as in l14 and `total_after(target, n)`, the float total of its first $n$ terms. For $T = -1$ the rule takes negatives first, then the large positive term 1. Check that after 2,000 terms the total is within 0.01 of $-1$.

tests.expect: [Fraction(-1, 2), Fraction(-1, 4), Fraction(-1, 6), Fraction(-1, 8), Fraction(1, 1), Fraction(-1, 10), Fraction(-1, 12), Fraction(-1, 14), Fraction(-1, 16), Fraction(-1, 18)]
[Fraction(1, 1), Fraction(1, 3), Fraction(1, 5), Fraction(-1, 2), Fraction(1, 7), Fraction(1, 9), Fraction(1, 11), Fraction(1, 13), Fraction(1, 15), Fraction(-1, 4), Fraction(1, 17), Fraction(1, 19)]

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Four are exact lists (targets -1, 3/2 and 0). One checks Fractions only. One checks the float total after 2,000 terms for target -1 within absolute 1e-9. One checks it is within 0.01 of -1. One checks that total_after returns a float.

feedback.correct: Right. After 2,000 terms the total is -0.9958.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from a total of 0, which is above $-1$, so the first terms are negative.

explain.text: From 0 the rule takes $-\tfrac12, -\tfrac14, -\tfrac16, -\tfrac18$, reaching $-1.0417$, then the positive 1 jumps to $-0.0417$. The swings shrink as the crossing terms do. After 2,000 terms the total is -0.9958, within 0.005 of $-1$.

items.title: The alternating series test, in full
items.prompt:
(a) Let $(a_n)$ be decreasing with $a_n \to 0$, and $S_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k+1} a_k$. Prove that $\sum (-1)^{n+1} a_n$ converges. Then prove that its sum $S$ satisfies $|S - S_n| \le a_{n+1}$ for every $n$.

(b) Use (a) to bound $|\ln 2 - S_{20}|$ for $\sum \tfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$, whose sum is $\ln 2$. Compare with the true error, $|\ln 2 - S_{20}| \approx 0.024376$.

Give a reason for every line.
items.model:
**(a) Claim.** If $a_n$ decreases to 0, then $\sum (-1)^{n+1} a_n$ converges to some $S$ with $|S - S_n| \le a_{n+1}$.

**Step 1: the even sums rise.** $S_{2n+2} - S_{2n} = a_{2n+1} - a_{2n+2} \ge 0$, since $(a_n)$ is decreasing.

**Step 2: the odd sums fall.** $S_{2n+1} - S_{2n-1} = -a_{2n} + a_{2n+1} \le 0$, again since $(a_n)$ is decreasing.

**Step 3: every even sum is below every odd sum.** $S_{2k+1} - S_{2k} = a_{2k+1} \ge 0$. For any $m, n$ let $k = \max(m, n)$. By steps 1 and 2, $S_{2m} \le S_{2k} \le S_{2k+1} \le S_{2n+1}$.

**Step 4: both strands converge.** By step 3 the even sums are bounded above by $S_1$, and by step 1 they rise. By the monotone convergence theorem $S_{2n} \to E$. Likewise the odd sums fall and are bounded below by $S_2$, so $S_{2n+1} \to O$.

**Step 5: the limits agree.** $O - E = \lim (S_{2n+1} - S_{2n}) = \lim a_{2n+1} = 0$, by the difference law and $a_n \to 0$. Write $S = O = E$.

**Step 6: the whole sequence converges.** Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose $N_1$ with $|S_{2n} - S| < \varepsilon$ for $n \ge N_1$, and $N_2$ with $|S_{2n+1} - S| < \varepsilon$ for $n \ge N_2$. For $n \ge 2\max(N_1, N_2) + 1$, $S_n$ is a term of one strand past its threshold, so $|S_n - S| < \varepsilon$. So $S_n \to S$. $\blacksquare$

**Error bound.** The even sums rise to $S$ and the odd sums fall to $S$, so $S_{2m} \le S \le S_{2m+1}$ for every $m$. Hence $S$ lies between any two neighbours $S_n$ and $S_{n+1}$, which differ by $a_{n+1}$. So $|S - S_n| \le |S_{n+1} - S_n| = a_{n+1}$.

**(b)** Here $a_n = \tfrac1n$ decreases to 0, so (a) applies with $S = \ln 2$. The bound is $|\ln 2 - S_{20}| \le a_{21} = \tfrac{1}{21} \approx 0.047619$. With $S_{20} \approx 0.668771$ and $\ln 2 \approx 0.693147$, the true error is about 0.024376, roughly half the bound. The bound is safe, not sharp: the true error is close to $\tfrac{1}{2n} = 0.025$.

rubric.text: Shows the even partial sums increase and the odd ones decrease, using that $(a_n)$ is decreasing.
Shows every even sum is at most every odd sum (through $k = \max(m, n)$), so each strand is bounded.
Applies monotone convergence to each strand and proves the limits agree using $a_n \to 0$.
Concludes that the whole sequence $(S_n)$ converges, covering both even and odd indices with one $N$.
Proves $|S - S_n| \le a_{n+1}$ from $S$ lying between $S_n$ and $S_{n+1}$.
(b) Checks the hypotheses for $\tfrac1n$, gives the bound $\tfrac1{21} \approx 0.0476$, and compares with the true error 0.0244.

items.title: The integral test, proved and used
items.prompt:
Let $m$ be a whole number and $f: [m, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ be positive, continuous and decreasing, with $a_n = f(n)$. Suppose $\int_m^X f(x)\,dx$ tends to a finite limit $I$ as $X \to \infty$.

(a) Prove that $\sum_{n \ge m} a_n$ converges. Then prove that for every whole number $K \ge m$ the tail satisfies $\sum_{n > K} a_n \le \int_K^\infty f(x)\,dx$.

(b) Prove that $\sum_{n \ge 2} \tfrac{1}{n(\ln n)^2}$ converges. Show that the ratio test cannot decide it.

(c) For this series, how large must $K$ be for your bound to promise a tail below 0.1? Give the smallest such $K$ and check it. Optional, one more point: use a lower bound for the tail to say how far that $K$ can be from the true smallest one.

Give a reason for every line. You may use these facts about integrals: a continuous function on $[p, q]$ has an integral there; if $g \le h$ on $[p, q]$ then $\int_p^q g \le \int_p^q h$; $\int_p^q c\,dx = c(q - p)$; $\int_p^q + \int_q^r = \int_p^r$; and $\int_p^q F' = F(q) - F(p)$ for a continuous $F'$.
items.model:
**(a)** $f$ is continuous, so every integral below exists. Write $S_n = a_m + \cdots + a_n$ for $n \ge m$.

*Each term against the integral.* Let $k \ge m + 1$. For $x \in [k - 1, k]$, $f(x) \ge f(k) = a_k$, since $f$ decreases. Comparing with the constant $a_k$ on an interval of width 1, $a_k \le \int_{k-1}^{k} f(x)\,dx$.

*Bounded partial sums.* Adding for $k = m + 1, \dots, n$ and joining the intervals, $S_n - a_m \le \int_m^n f(x)\,dx$. Let $F(X) = \int_m^X f$. For $X < Y$, $F(Y) - F(X) = \int_X^Y f \ge 0$, since $f > 0$, so $F$ increases. An increasing $F$ with limit $I$ never exceeds $I$: if $F(X_0) > I$, then $F(X) \ge F(X_0)$ for all $X \ge X_0$, and $F$ could not tend to $I$. So $S_n \le a_m + I$ for every $n$.

*Convergence.* $S_{n+1} = S_n + a_{n+1} > S_n$, since $f > 0$. So $(S_n)$ is increasing and bounded above, and it converges by the monotone convergence theorem. Call its limit $S$. $\blacksquare$

*The tail.* Let $K \ge m$. Then $\int_K^X f = F(X) - F(K)$ increases in $X$ to $I - F(K)$, which is $\int_K^\infty f$. Let $n > K$. Adding the term bound for $k = K + 1, \dots, n$, $S_n - S_K \le \int_K^n f \le \int_K^\infty f$, the last step as for $F$ above. As $n \to \infty$ the left side tends to $S - S_K = \sum_{n > K} a_n$. Limits keep $\le$, so $\sum_{n > K} a_n \le \int_K^\infty f(x)\,dx$. $\blacksquare$

**(b)** Let $f(x) = \tfrac{1}{x(\ln x)^2}$ on $[2, \infty)$, so $m = 2$.

*Hypotheses.* For $x \ge 2$, $\ln x \ge \ln 2 > 0$. So the denominator is positive: $f > 0$, and $f$ is continuous as a quotient of continuous functions. Both $x$ and $(\ln x)^2$ are positive and increasing there, so their product increases and $f$ decreases.

*The integral.* By the chain rule, $\tfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\tfrac{1}{\ln x}\right) = \tfrac{1}{(\ln x)^2} \cdot \tfrac1x = f(x)$. So $\int_2^X f = \tfrac{1}{\ln 2} - \tfrac{1}{\ln X}$. As $X \to \infty$, $\ln X \to \infty$, since $\ln$ increases and $\ln X > M$ once $X > e^M$, so this tends to $I = \tfrac{1}{\ln 2} \approx 1.4427$. By (a) the series converges, and its tail after $K$ is at most $\int_K^\infty f = \tfrac{1}{\ln K}$.

*The ratio test is silent.* $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \tfrac{n}{n+1}\left(\tfrac{\ln n}{\ln(n+1)}\right)^2$. First, $\tfrac{n}{n+1} = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n+1} \to 1$.

Next, for $t > 0$, $\ln(1 + t) = \int_1^{1+t} \tfrac{dx}{x} \le \int_1^{1+t} 1\,dx = t$, since $\tfrac1x \le 1$ there. So $0 < \ln(n + 1) - \ln n = \ln\left(1 + \tfrac1n\right) \le \tfrac1n$. Dividing by $\ln(n + 1) \ge \ln n > 0$ gives $1 - \tfrac{1}{n \ln n} \le \tfrac{\ln n}{\ln(n+1)} < 1$.

Since $\tfrac{1}{n \ln n} \le \tfrac{1}{n \ln 2}$, and $\tfrac1n \to 0$ by the Archimedean property, the squeeze gives $\tfrac{\ln n}{\ln(n+1)} \to 1$. By the product law the ratios tend to $1 \cdot 1^2 = 1$. The ratio test decides nothing when the limit is 1.

**(c)** The bound promises a tail below 0.1 when $\tfrac{1}{\ln K} < 0.1$, that is $\ln K > 10$, or $K > e^{10} \approx 22026.47$. So the smallest such $K$ is 22,027. Check: $\ln 22027 \approx 10.000024 > 10$, while $\ln 22026 \approx 9.999979 < 10$, so the bound does not cover $K = 22026$.

*A lower bound.* For $x \in [k, k + 1]$, $f(x) \le f(k) = a_k$, since $f$ decreases, so $a_k \ge \int_k^{k+1} f$. Adding for $k = K + 1, \dots, n$ and letting $n \to \infty$, the tail after $K$ is at least $\int_{K+1}^\infty f = \tfrac{1}{\ln(K + 1)}$.

For $K \le 22025$, $K + 1 \le 22026 < e^{10}$, so the tail is at least $\tfrac{1}{\ln(K + 1)} > 0.1$. So the true smallest $K$ is 22,026 or 22,027, and the bound is off by at most one. The series is very slow: it needs over 22,000 terms to get within 0.1.

rubric.text: (a) Bounds each term, $a_k \le \int_{k-1}^{k} f$, because $f$ decreases. Sums to $S_n \le a_m + I$, saying why $\int_m^n f \le I$ ($f > 0$, so the integral grows with its end). Then $(S_n)$ increases as $a_n > 0$, and converges by monotone convergence.
(a) Proves the tail bound: $\sum_{k = K+1}^{n} a_k \le \int_K^n f \le \int_K^\infty f$ for the finite sum, then lets $n \to \infty$, since limits keep $\le$.

(b) Tick only if all are given. $f(x) = \tfrac{1}{x(\ln x)^2}$ meets the three hypotheses on $[2, \infty)$, with reasons. $\int_2^X f = \tfrac{1}{\ln 2} - \tfrac{1}{\ln X} \to \tfrac{1}{\ln 2}$, so the series converges. The ratios tend to 1, with $\tfrac{\ln n}{\ln(n+1)} \to 1$ justified, so the ratio test is silent.
(c) Gives $K = 22027$ from $\tfrac{1}{\ln K} < 0.1$, that is $K > e^{10} \approx 22026.47$, and checks that the bound does not cover 22,026.
(c) Proves the lower bound $\tfrac{1}{\ln(K + 1)}$ for the tail, and concludes that no $K \le 22025$ works, so the true smallest $K$ is 22,026 or 22,027.
